text: The Panavia Tornado is a family of twin-engine, variable-sweep wing multi-role combat aircraft jointly developed and manufactured by Italy, the United Kingdom, and Germany. It consists of three primary variants: the Tornado IDS (interdictor/strike) fighter-bomber, the Tornado ECR (electronic combat/reconnaissance) SEAD aircraft, and the Tornado ADV (air defence variant) interceptor. Developed by Panavia Aircraft GmbH, a tri-national consortium comprising British Aerospace (formerly British Aircraft Corporation), MBB of West Germany, and Aeritalia of Italy, the Tornado first flew on 14 August 1974 and entered service between 1979 and 1980. Due to its multirole capabilities, it replaced several different aircraft types in the air forces of its operators. The Royal Saudi Air Force (RSAF) is the only export operator of the Tornado, in addition to the three original partner nations. A training and evaluation unit, the Tri-National Tornado Training Establishment (TTTE), operated from RAF Cottesmore and maintained international cooperation beyond production. The Tornado is the only non-American-developed aircraft currently approved to carry United States nuclear weapons under NATO's Nuclear Planning Group. The Tornado was operated by the Royal Air Force (RAF), Italian Air Force, and RSAF during the Gulf War of 1991, conducting numerous low-altitude penetrating strike missions. It was also used in the Bosnian War, Kosovo War, Iraq War, the 2011 Libyan civil war, and in smaller roles in Afghanistan, Yemen, and Syria. Including all variants, 990 aircraft were built. The concept of variable-geometry wings was explored in the 1960s to combine the maneuverability of straight wings with the speed of swept wings. The UK cancelled the BAC TSR-2 and the US F-111K in 1965 and 1967, respectively, and sought a replacement for the Avro Vulcan and Blackburn Buccaneer. Britain and France initiated the BAC/Dassault AFVG project in 1965, which ended with French withdrawal in 1967. West Germany, the Netherlands, Belgium, Italy, and Canada formed a working group in 1968 to replace the Lockheed F-104G Starfighter, initially called the Multi Role Aircraft (MRA) and later renamed the Multi Role Combat Aircraft (MRCA). Due to diverse requirements, a single multirole aircraft was developed. Britain joined in 1968, and a memorandum of agreement was signed between the UK, West Germany, and Italy in May 1969. By the end of 1968, the six countries planned to purchase 1,500 aircraft. Canada and Belgium withdrew before long-term commitments; Canada found the project politically unpalatable, and France offered Belgium the Dassault Mirage 5. On 26 March 1969, the UK, Germany, Italy, and the Netherlands agreed to form Panavia Aircraft GmbH to develop and manufacture the MRCA. The project aimed to produce an aircraft capable of tactical strike, reconnaissance, air defence, and maritime missions. Various design concepts, including fixed-wing and single-engine options, were studied. The Netherlands withdrew in 1970, citing complexity, and Germany reduced its order from 600 to 324 in 1972. It is suggested Germany initially placed a high order to secure design influence in Germany. The UK and West Germany each held a 42.5% share of the workload, with Italy holding 15%, influenced by political negotiations. The front fuselage and tail were assigned to BAC (now BAE Systems), the centre fuselage to MBB (now part of Airbus), and the wings to Aeritalia (now Leonardo). A separate company, Turbo-Union, formed in June 1970, developed the RB199 engines with ownership split 40% Rolls-Royce, 40% MTU, and 20% FIAT. In May 1970, two designs were selected: the single-seat Panavia 100 and the twin-seat Panavia 200, with the latter preferred by the RAF. The aircraft was briefly called the Panavia Panther. In September 1971, the three governments signed an Intention to Proceed (ITP) document, designating the aircraft for low-level strike missions, with the UK's Chief of the Defence Staff stating that two-thirds of the front-line fighting force would consist of this aircraft. The first of fifteen development aircraft, including nine prototypes (P01 to P09) and six pre-series (PS11 to PS16), flew on 14 August 1974 at Manching, Germany. Pilot Paul Millett described the flight as smooth and almost simulated. Flight testing required modifications, including re-profiling engine intakes and fuselage to reduce surging and buffeting at supersonic speeds. Jim Quinn, a developer of the Tornado simulation software and engine controls, noted that the prototype could reach supercruise safely, but engines had safety issues at high altitude during deceleration due to combustion pressure backfiring; engine controls automatically increased idle settings with altitude, leading to one aircraft being stuck at Mach 1.2 and unable to decelerate. A nose-wheel steering augmentation system was needed to counteract destabilization during landing with the thrust reverser deployed. Two prototypes were lost due to pilot error in ground collisions, and a third was seriously damaged by pilot-induced pitch oscillation. Designers incorporated advanced stability augmentation systems and autopilots, similar to those in the F-16. Failure testing of the triplex analogue CSAS was conducted on flight control rigs, complicated by variable-sweep wings and heavy payloads. The contract for Batch 1 aircraft was signed on 29 July 1976. The first production aircraft flew on 10 July 1979 at BAe Warton, with the first deliveries to the RAF and German Air Force on 5 and 6 June 1979, respectively. The first Italian Tornado was delivered on 25 September 1981. The TTTE officially opened on 29 January 1981 and remained active until 31 March 1999. The 500th Tornado was delivered to West Germany on 19 December 1987. Saudi Arabia was the only export customer, as part of the Al-Yamamah arms deal between British Aerospace and the Saudi government. Oman committed to purchasing eight Tornado F2s and associated equipment for £250 million in August 1985 but cancelled the order in 1990 due to financial difficulties. Australia considered joining the MRCA programme to replace its Dassault Mirage IIIs and ultimately selected the F/A-18 Hornet. Canada also chose the F/A-18 after considering the Tornado. Japan considered the Tornado in the 1980s, along with the F-16 and F/A-18, before selecting the Mitsubishi F-2. In the 1990s, Taiwan and South Korea expressed interest in acquiring small numbers of Tornado ECR aircraft. In 2001, EADS proposed a Tornado ECR variant with enhanced electronic warfare capabilities for Australia. Production ended in 1998, with the final batch going to the RSAF, which ordered 96 IDS Tornados. In June 2011, the Tornado fleet collectively flew over one million flying hours. Aviation author Jon Lake noted that the Panavia consortium produced just under 1,000 Tornados, making it one of the most successful postwar bomber programs. In 2008, AirForces Monthly called the Tornado "for more than a quarter of a century... the most important military aircraft in Western Europe." The Tornado is designed as a low-level penetration aircraft with variable-sweep wings enabling efficient high-speed and low-speed flight. Its mission during the Cold War involved delivering conventional and nuclear weapons against Warsaw Pact forces in Eastern Europe. The variable wing geometry minimizes drag during low-level flight. Advanced navigation and flight computers, including a fly-by-wire system, reduce pilot workload. For long-range missions, it has a retractable refuelling probe. As a multirole aircraft, it replaced multiple specialized aircraft types with a single platform, either through standard Tornados or modified variants like the Tornado ECR. The most extensive modification was the Tornado ADV, which was stretched and armed with long-range anti-aircraft missiles for interception. Operators have conducted life extension and upgrade programs, projecting continued service until 2025. To perform as a low-level supersonic strike aircraft, the Tornado required good high- and low-speed flight characteristics. A swept or delta wing is efficient at high speed but inefficient at low speed; the variable-sweep wing enables performance at both speeds. The wing sweep angle ranges from 25 to 67 degrees, with each angle having a specific speed range. Some Tornado ADVs had an automatic wing-sweep system. When wings are swept back, drag is reduced, aiding high-speed low-level flight. Weapons pylons pivot with the wing sweep so stores point in the direction of flight. Significant attention was given to short-field take-off and landing (STOL) performance, particularly in Germany. The Tornado can sweep wings to 25 degrees, deploy full-span flaps and leading edge slats, and use thrust reversers for excellent low-speed handling. The aircraft has a tandem-seat cockpit with a pilot and navigator/weapons officer, using electromechanical and electro-optical controls. Dials and switches are mounted on either side of a centrally placed CRT monitor for navigation, communications, and weapons control. BAE Systems developed the Tornado Advanced Radar Display Information System (TARDIS), a 32.5-centimetre multi-function display, replacing the rear cockpit's Combined Radar and Projected Map Display; the RAF began installing it on the GR4 fleet in 2004. The primary flight controls are a fly-by-wire hybrid, consisting of an analogue quadruplex Command and Stability Augmentation System (CSAS) connected to a digital Autopilot & Flight Director System (AFDS), with mechanical reversion retained for safety. Artificial feel is built into the controls, adjusting automatically to wing profile and flight attitude changes. The flight stability system compensates for changes in flight dynamics due to a wide range of munitions. The Tornado has a combined navigation/attack Doppler radar that scans for targets and conducts fully automated terrain-following for all-weather, hands-off low-level flight. The Tornado ADV uses the AI.24 Foxhunter radar, capable of tracking up to 20 targets at ranges up to 160 kilometres (100 miles). The Tornado was one of the first aircraft to feature a digital data bus, with Link 16 JTIDS integration on the F3 variant enabling data exchange with friendly aircraft. The Tornado ECR, operated by Germany and Italy, is dedicated to Suppression of Enemy Air Defences (SEAD) and is equipped with an emitter-locator system (ELS) to detect radar use. German ECRs have a Honeywell infrared imaging system for reconnaissance. RAF and RSAF Tornados have the Laser Range Finder and Marked Target Seekers (LRMTS) for targeting laser-guided munitions. In 1991, the RAF introduced the Thermal Imaging and Laser Designator (TIALD) system.

The Tornado ADV features a different radar system, the AI.24 Foxhunter, designed for air defence operations, capable of tracking up to 20 targets at ranges of up to 160 kilometres (100 mi). It was one of the earliest aircraft to incorporate a digital data bus for data transmission, and the F3 variant includes Link 16 JTIDS integration, enabling the exchange of radar and sensory data with nearby friendly aircraft. Variants are equipped with mission-specific avionics: the German and Italian Tornado ECRs perform Suppression of Enemy Air Defences (SEAD) missions and are fitted with an emitter-locator system (ELS) to detect radar use; German ECRs also have a Honeywell infrared imaging system for reconnaissance. RAF and RSAF Tornados are equipped with Laser Range Finder and Marked Target Seekers (LRMTS) for targeting laser-guided munitions; in 1991, the RAF introduced the Thermal Imaging and Laser Designator (TIALD), allowing Tornado GR1s to laser-designate their own targets. The GR1A and GR4A reconnaissance variants use the Tornado Infrared Reconnaissance System (TIRRS), which includes one SLIR sensor on each side of the fuselage forward of the engine intakes for oblique images and a single IRLS sensor on the underside for vertical images, with images recorded on six S-VHS video tapes; the RAPTOR reconnaissance pod replaced the built-in TIRRS system. The Tornado can carry a wide range of NATO air-launched weapons, including unguided and laser-guided bombs, anti-ship and anti-radiation missiles, and specialized munitions like anti-personnel mines and anti-runway weapons. To enhance combat survivability, it is equipped with onboard countermeasures such as flare and chaff dispensers and electronic countermeasure pods mounted under the wings; underwing fuel tanks and a buddy store aerial refuelling system allow range extension. Since its introduction, operators have conducted various upgrades to deploy new weapons, including the Enhanced Paveway and Joint Direct Attack Munition bombs and modern cruise missiles such as the Taurus and Storm Shadow, improving combat accuracy and capabilities; precision cruise missiles have replaced older munitions like cluster bombs. Strike variants have limited air-to-air capability with AIM-9 Sidewinder or AIM-132 ASRAAM missiles; the Tornado ADV is equipped with beyond visual range AAMs such as Skyflash and AIM-120 AMRAAM. The Tornado has two internally mounted 27 mm (1.063 in) Mauser BK-27 revolver cannons under the fuselage; the ADV variant has only one. When RAF GR1s were converted to GR4s, the FLIR sensor replaced the left cannon, leaving only one; the GR1A reconnaissance variant gave up both guns to accommodate sideways-looking infra-red sensors. The Mauser BK-27 was developed specifically for the Tornado and has since been used on other European fighters, including the Alpha Jet, JAS 39 Gripen, and Eurofighter Typhoon. The Tornado is capable of delivering air-launched nuclear weapons; in 1979, Britain considered replacing its Polaris submarines with either Trident or the Tornado as the primary nuclear deterrent, though it proceeded with Trident; several Tornado squadrons in Germany were assigned to SACEUR to deter a major Soviet offensive using conventional and nuclear weapons, including the WE.177, which was retired in 1998; German and Italian Tornados can deliver US B61 nuclear bombs through NATO. Britain insisted on Rolls-Royce developing the advanced engine for the MRCA, opposing American engine adoption, and in September 1969, Rolls-Royce's RB199 engine was selected; a technology transfer agreement led to joint development and manufacturing by Turbo-Union. The programme was delayed by Rolls-Royce's entry into receivership in 1971, but multinational collaboration prevented major disruption; research from the Concorde contributed to the RB199 and engine control unit development. The Tornado uses variable intake ramps to maximize air pressure entering the engine up to Mach 2; each engine drives an airframe gearbox with an electrical generator, hydraulic pump, and fuel boost pump, with both generators and hydraulic pumps capable of being driven by a single engine; in case of double-engine or double-generator failure, an emergency battery operates one fuel and one hydraulic pump for up to 13 minutes. The RB199 includes a thrust reverser to reduce landing distance, with a yaw damper connected to the nosewheel steering for greater stability when used. The first RB199 flight occurred under a Vulcan in April 1973; the first Tornado prototype, P01, flew on 14 August 1974 from Ingolstadt Manching Airport, West Germany, and the engine completed qualification tests in late 1978; the final production engine met reliability and performance standards, though development costs exceeded predictions due to ambitious performance requirements; early turbine blades had a shorter life, corrected by design revisions; several uprated engines were developed and used on most Tornado ADVs and German ECRs; the DECU (Digital Engine Control Unit) is the current engine control unit, replacing the analogue MECU (Main Engine Control Unit) or CUE. Designed for low-level operations, the Tornado required modifications for medium-level operations adopted by the RAF in the 1990s; the RAF re-manufactured its GR1 fleet into GR4s with upgrades including forward-looking infrared, a wide-angle HUD, improved cockpit displays, NVG capabilities, new avionics, and a GPS receiver, easing integration of new weapons and sensors such as the Storm Shadow cruise missile, Brimstone anti-tank missile, Paveway III bombs, and RAPTOR pod; the first GR4 flight was on 4 April 1997, with the first delivery on 31 October 1997 and completion of deliveries in 2003; in 2005, the RSAF upgraded its IDS fleet to match the RAF's GR4 configuration; in December 2007, BAE signed a £210m contract for CUSP, the Capability Upgrade Strategy (Pilot), which included integrating the Paveway IV bomb and a communications upgrade in Phase A, followed by a new tactical datalink in Phase B. German IDS and ECR Tornados began receiving the ASSTA 1 upgrade in 2000, which included a new weapons computer, GPS, and Laser Inertial navigation systems, enabling integration of HARM missiles, Taurus KEPD 350 missiles, Rafael Litening II pod, and Paveway III bombs; ASSTA 2, beginning in 2005, included new digital avionics and an ECM suite, applied to 85 aircraft (20 ECRs and 65 IDSs), as the Tornado is being phased out by the Eurofighter Typhoon; ASSTA 3, started in 2008, adds support for the laser-targeted Joint Direct Attack Munition and further software changes. In January 2016, Bild reported that the ASSTA 3.1 upgrade, featuring colour multifunctional LCD screens replacing monochrome CRT displays, interfered with helmet-mounted night-vision displays, rendering German Tornado bombers in Syria ineffective for night missions; the defence ministry acknowledged bright cockpit lights could distract pilots and said a solution would be implemented soon, but denied the need for night missions in Syria. TV TAB displays are used for route planning, FLIR sensors, and targeting pods such as TIALD and CLDP; the original MRCA TV TAB DU display (part number V22.498.90) uses a green CRT with a price of €33,852.64 per unit; high brightness levels caused CRT wear; an Active Matrix Liquid Crystal Display (AMLCD) drop-fit replacement (NSN 5895-99-597-1323) was developed to reduce lifecycle costs, featuring a color display and a bezel that reduces the viewing angle; the AMLCD has a built-in menu for selecting GR1, GR4, or F3, self-test, and display tests; the original CRT has two white domes with light sensors and white buttons, while the AMLCD has black buttons with white dots; the AMLCD requires only 28 VDC, unlike the CRT which needed both 115 VAC 400 Hz and 28 VDC, with a separate HVPS for the CRT; the AMLCD has a built-in 115 VAC to 28 VDC converter and no HVPS; it has a diagnostic connector and is considered a 'dumb' device compared to the original CRT, which only required a video signal and external waveform generator; the AMLCD has a self-test and display test features. In December 2013, BAE Systems test-flown a Tornado with 3D-printed parts, including a radio cover, landing-gear guard, and air-intake door support struts, demonstrating the feasibility of producing replacement parts quickly and cheaply at air bases; parts cost less than £100 to make, saving over £300,000, with potential savings reaching over £1.2 million by 2017. The first Tornado prototype flew on 14 August 1974 from Ingolstadt Manching Airport, West Germany; production deliveries began on 27 July 1979; a total of 247 Tornados were delivered to the German Air Force, including 35 ECR variants; originally, Tornados equipped five fighter-bomber wings, one tactical conversion unit, and four front-line wings, replacing the F-104 Starfighter; when one of the two German Navy Tornado wings was disbanded in 1994, its aircraft were used to re-equip a Luftwaffe reconnaissance wing previously equipped with RF-4E Phantoms. Fourteen German Tornados conducted combat operations during the Bosnian War as part of NATO's campaign, flying reconnaissance missions from Piacenza, Italy, to survey damage and scout new targets, significantly improving target selection. In 1999, German Tornados participated in Operation Allied Force, NATO's airstrikes against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia during the Kosovo War, marking Germany's first offensive air mission since WWII; ECRs escorted allied aircraft and carried AGM-88 HARM missiles to counter enemy radar; during the Kosovo conflict, IDS Tornados conducted reconnaissance to identify enemy ground forces and civilian refugees, flying 2108 hours and 446 sorties and firing 236 HARM missiles. In June 2007, two Luftwaffe Tornados flew reconnaissance missions over an anti-globalisation demonstration during the 33rd G8 summit in Heiligendamm; the German Defence Ministry admitted one aircraft breached the minimum flying altitude and acknowledged handling errors in summit security. In 2007, a detachment of six Tornados from Aufklärungsgeschwader 51 "Immelmann" was deployed to Mazar-i-Sharif, Northern Afghanistan, to support NATO forces; the deployment was controversial, with one political party launching an unsuccessful legal challenge; improvements to reconnaissance equipment were accelerated to enhance detection of hidden improvised explosive devices (IEDs); the German Tornados were withdrawn from Afghanistan in November 2010. Defence cuts announced in March 2003 led to the retirement of 90 Tornados, reducing Luftwaffe strength to four wings by September 2005; on 13 January 2004, German Defence Minister Peter Struck announced a plan to reduce the fighter fleet from 426 in early 2004 to 265 by 2015, reducing the Tornado force to 85, with the type expected to remain in service until 2025; the retained aircraft are undergoing a service life extension programme. Currently, the Luftwaffe operates Tornados with Tactical Wings Taktisches Luftwaffengeschwader 33 at Cochem/Büchel Air Base, Rhineland-Palatinate, and Taktisches Luftwaffengeschwader 51 "Immelmann" at Jagel, Schleswig-Holstein. German Tornado aircrew training took place at Holloman Air Force Base in New Mexico, US, starting in January 1996, at the Taktische Ausbildungskommando der Luftwaffe USA (TaktAusbKdoLw USA), which trained both German F-4 Phantom and Tornado crews.

A major part of the German defence announcement involved reducing the fighter fleet from 426 in early 2004 to 265 by 2015, with the German Tornado force to be cut to 85, and the aircraft expected to remain in service with the Luftwaffe until 2025. The retained Tornados are undergoing a service life extension programme. Currently, the Luftwaffe operates Tornados with Tactical Wings Taktisches Luftwaffengeschwader 33 at Cochem/Büchel Air Base in Rhineland-Palatinate and Taktisches Luftwaffengeschwader 51 "Immelmann" at Jagel in Schleswig-Holstein. German Tornado aircrew training previously took place at Holloman Air Force Base in New Mexico, US, from January 1996 through the Taktische Ausbildungskommando der Luftwaffe USA, which trained both German F-4 Phantom and Tornado crews; in 1999, the command was renamed Fliegerisches Ausbildungszentrum der Luftwaffe. In March 2015, Defence Minister Ursula von der Leyen decided to continue this training in Germany. In September 2017, flight training at Holloman for the Tornado was discontinued and transferred to Taktisches Luftwaffengeschwader 51 in Jagel, with the US location command dissolved in 2019. In April 2020, the German defence ministry planned to replace its Tornado fleet with 30 Boeing F/A-18E/F Super Hornets, 15 EA-18G Growlers, and 55 Eurofighter Typhoons, selecting the Super Hornet due to its compatibility with nuclear weapons and availability of an electronic attack version. In March 2020, the Super Hornet was not certified for the B61 nuclear bombs, though Dan Gillian, head of Boeing's Super Hornet program, stated that the German requirements could be met with U.S. government collaboration on the required timeline. In 2021, Airbus offered to replace 90 ageing Tornado IDS and ECR aircraft with 85 new Eurofighter Tranche 5 standard from 2030. In 2022, the German defence ministry announced that 35 Lockheed Martin F-35 Lightning IIs would replace the Tornado fleet for nuclear sharing instead of the previously discussed 30 Boeing Super Hornets. In addition to the Luftwaffe order, the German Navy's Marineflieger received 112 IDS variants for anti-ship and marine reconnaissance roles, replacing the Starfighter, with two wings each having a nominal strength of 48 aircraft. The principal anti-ship weapon was the AS.34 Kormoran missile, initially supplemented by unguided bombs and BL755 cluster munitions, later by AGM-88 HARM anti-radar missiles, and reconnaissance missions used pods with panoramic optical cameras and infrared line scan. Following the end of the Cold War and the CFE Treaty, Germany reduced its armed forces, including combat aircraft; one Marineflieger Tornado wing was disbanded on 1 January 1994, with its aircraft replacing a Luftwaffe reconnaissance wing's Phantoms, and the second wing was enlarged and continued in anti-shipping, reconnaissance, and anti-radar roles until disbanded in 2005, with its aircraft and duties transferred to the Luftwaffe. The first Italian prototype of the Tornado made its maiden flight on 5 December 1975 from Turin; the Aeronautica Militare received 100 Tornado IDSs (known as A-200 in Italian service), with 16 converted to ECR configuration; the first Italian Tornado ECR (EA-200) was delivered on 27 February 1998. As a stop-gap, the Aeronautica Militare operated 24 Tornado ADVs in the air defence role, leased from the RAF to cover the gap between the retirement of the F-104 Starfighter and the introduction of the Eurofighter Typhoon. Italian Tornados, along with RAF Tornados, participated in the first Gulf War in 1991, with eight IDS interdictors deployed from Gioia del Colle to Al Dhafra, Abu Dhabi, as part of Italy's coalition contribution; one aircraft was lost to Iraqi anti-aircraft fire, with pilots ejecting safely and being captured. A total of 22 Italian Tornados were deployed in Operation Allied Force over Kosovo in 1999; A-200s served in bombing and EA-200s in radar suppression, firing 115 AGM-88 HARM missiles. In 2000, due to Eurofighter delays, Italy began searching for an interim fighter; while the Tornado was considered, long-term lease extensions requiring RAF CSP upgrades were deemed cost ineffective. In February 2001, Italy announced a lease of 35 F-16s from the US under the PEACE CAESAR programme. The Aeronautica Militare returned its Tornado ADVs to the RAF, with the final aircraft arriving at RAF St Athan on 7 December 2004; one was retained for static display at the Italian Air Force Museum. In July 2002, Italy signed a contract with the Tornado Management Agency (NETMA) and Panavia to upgrade 18 A-200s, the first received in 2003; the upgrade included improved navigation systems (integrated GPS and laser INS) and new weapons such as the Storm Shadow cruise missile, Joint Direct Attack Munition, and Paveway III laser-guided bombs. In response to anticipated violence during the 2010 Afghanistan elections, Italy dispatched four A-200 Tornados; it opted to extend the Tornado's service life over alternatives like the AMX, initiating a major upgrade and life extension programme in 2010 to include digital displays, Link 16 communications, night-vision goggles compatibility, and other upgrades. In the long term, Italy plans to replace its Tornado IDS/ECR fleet with the F-35 Lightning II, with the final Italian Tornado scheduled to be phased out in 2025; the first of 15 upgraded Tornado EA-200s was received on 15 June 2013. Italian Tornado A-200 and EA-200 aircraft participated in the UN no-fly zone enforcement during the 2011 Libya intervention; various coalition aircraft operated from Italy, including RAF Tornados; Italian military aircraft delivered 710 guided bombs and missiles, with 550 from A-200s and AMXs and 160 from Navy AV-8Bs; Tornados launched 20 to 30 Storm Shadow cruise missiles, the rest being Paveway and JDAM guided bombs. On 19 August 2014, two Italian Tornados collided mid-air during a training mission near Ascoli. On 14 November 2014, Italy announced it was sending four Tornado aircraft with 135 support staff to Ahmad al-Jaber Air Base and two other bases in Kuwait for coalition operations against the Islamic State, using them for reconnaissance only. In October 2018, the EA-200 Tornado successfully completed operational testing of the AGM-88E AARGM, providing capabilities including expanded target set, counter-shutdown, advanced signals processing, geographic specificity, and weapon impact-assessment broadcast. Nicknamed the "Tonka" by the British, the first Tornado prototype (XX946) made its maiden flight on 30 October 1974 from BAC Warton; the first full production Tornado GR1 (ZA319) flew on 10 July 1979 from Warton; the first RAF Tornados (ZA320 and ZA322) were delivered to the TTTE at RAF Cottesmore on 1 July 1980. Crews qualified from the TTTE went to the Tornado Weapons Conversion Unit (TWCU), formed on 1 August 1981 at RAF Honington, before being posted to front-line squadrons. No. IX (B) Squadron became the first front-line squadron in the world to operate the Tornado upon reformation on 1 June 1982, receiving its first Tornado GR1 ZA586 on 6 January 1982; it was declared strike combat ready to SACEUR in January 1983. Two more squadrons were formed at RAF Marham in 1983—No. 617 Squadron on 1 January and No. 27 Squadron on 12 August. The first RAF Tornado GR1 loss occurred on 27 September 1983 when ZA586 suffered complete electrical failure and crashed; navigator Flt. Lt. Nigel Nickles ejected but pilot Sqn. Ldr. Michael Stephens died after ordering ejection. In January 1984, the TWCU became No. 45 (Reserve) Squadron. RAF Germany (RAFG) began receiving Tornados with the formation of No. XV (Designate) Squadron on 1 September 1983 at RAF Laarbruch, followed by No. 16 (Designate) Squadron in January 1984 (both former Buccaneer squadrons), and No. 20 (Designate) Squadron in May 1984 (operating SEPECAT Jaguar GR1 from RAF Brüggen). Unlike UK-based Tornado squadrons under British control, RAFG squadrons were under SACEUR, with aircraft on Quick Reaction Alert (Nuclear), "QRA (N)", equipped with the WE.177 nuclear bomb; in the event of a 'hot' Cold War, the majority were tasked with destroying Warsaw Pact airfields and SAM sites in East Germany; No. 20 Squadron had a separate mission to destroy bridges over the Elbe and Weser rivers. By early 1985, Nos. XV, 16, and 20 Squadrons at RAF Laarbruch were declared strike combat ready to SACEUR. Tornados began arriving at RAF Brüggen in September 1984 with No. 31 (Designate) Squadron, No. 17 (Designate) Squadron formed in December 1984, and No. 14 (Designate) Squadron in mid-1985. No. IX (B) Squadron relocated from RAF Honington to RAF Brüggen on 1 October 1986, arriving in a diamond formation. The Reykjavík Summit in October 1986 ended QRA (Nuclear) for the Tornado force. By the end of 1986, the Tornado GR1 fleet had been equipped with a Laser Ranger and Marked Target Seeker (LRMTS) under the nose and began receiving BOZ-107 chaff and flare dispensers. The Tornado made its combat debut in Operation Granby, the British contribution to the Gulf War in 1991, with 49 RAF Tornado GR1s deployed to Muharraq Airfield in Bahrain and to Tabuk and Dhahran Air Bases in Saudi Arabia. Eighteen Tornado F3s were deployed to provide air cover, deterring Iraqi pilots with long-range missiles. Early in the conflict, GR1s targeted Iraqi airfields using 450 kg unguided bombs in loft-bombing and JP233 runway denial weapons. On 17 January 1991, the first Tornado was shot down by an Iraqi SA-16 missile after a failed low-level bombing run; on 19 January, another was shot down during an intensive raid on Tallil Air Base. Six RAF Tornados were lost in the conflict—four with unguided bombs, one after JP233, and one attempting to deliver laser-guided bombs. The UK sent a detachment of Buccaneer aircraft with Pave Spike laser designators to allow Tornado GR1s to drop precision-guided weapons; a programme to fit GR1s with the TIALD laser designation system was accelerated, enabling the GR1 to achieve "probably the most accurate bombing in the RAF's history," according to Claus-Christian Szejnmann. Although effective, only 23 TIALD pods were purchased by 2000, causing shortages during operations over Kosovo. After the war's opening phase, GR1s switched to medium-level strike missions targeting munition depots and oil refineries; only the reconnaissance GR1As continued low-altitude, high-speed missions without incident. After the conflict, Britain maintained a military presence in the Gulf, with around six GR1s based at Ali Al Salem airbase in Kuwait contributing to the southern no-fly zone under Operation Southern Watch and six additional GR1s participating in Operation Provide Comfort over Northern Iraq. The upgraded Tornado GR4 made its operational debut in Operation Southern Watch, patrolling Iraq's southern airspace from Kuwait. Both GR1s and GR4s based at Ali Al Salem participated in coalition strikes during Operation Desert Fox in 1998. In December 1998, an Iraqi anti-aircraft battery fired six to eight missiles at a patrolling Tornado; the battery was later attacked in retaliation, with no aircraft lost. It was reported that during Desert Fox, RAF Tornados successfully destroyed 75% of their targets, with 28 of 36 planned missions completed. The GR1 participated in the Kosovo War in 1999, initially operating from RAF Brüggen and later from Solenzara Air Base, Corsica. Experiences from Kosovo led to the RAF procuring AGM-65 Maverick missiles and Enhanced Paveway smart bombs. Following the Kosovo War, the GR1 was phased out as aircraft were upgraded to GR4 standard; the final upgrade was returned to the RAF on 10 June 2003. The GR4 was used in Operation Telic, Britain's contribution to the 2003 invasion of Iraq, flying alongside American aircraft in the opening phase, striking Iraqi targets. Aiming to minimize civilian casualties, Tornados deployed the Storm Shadow cruise missile for the first time; while 25% of UK air-launched weapons in Kosovo were precision-guided, this ratio increased to 85% in Iraq. On 23 March 2003, a Tornado GR4 was shot down over Iraq by friendly fire from a US Patriot missile battery, killing both crew members. In July 2003, a US board of inquiry exonerated the battery's operators, noting the Tornado's "lack of functioning IFF (Identification Friend or Foe)."

The RAF operated Tornado GR1 and GR4 variants, with the GR1 initially entering service in the early 1980s, the first aircraft delivered on 5 June 1979. The GR1B, a specialized anti-shipping variant, replaced the Buccaneer, with 26 aircraft converted and based at RAF Lossiemouth, each capable of carrying up to four Sea Eagle anti-ship missiles; early GR1Bs lacked radar for tracking shipping and relied on missile seekers, later upgraded to pass target data from aircraft to missile. A single GR1 (ZA326) was rebuilt into a GR1P after a fire during testing and served with the Royal Aircraft Establishment and Empire Test Pilot's School until retired in 2005, becoming the last GR1 in service globally. The UK Ministry of Defence began studies for a GR1 Mid-Life Update in 1984, and in 1994, a GR4 upgrade was approved to improve medium-altitude capabilities based on lessons from the 1991 Gulf War. British Aerospace (later BAE Systems) upgraded 142 GR1s to GR4 standard between 1996 and 2003. Fifty-nine RAF GR4s later received the CUSP avionics upgrade, achieving Initial Service Date in March 2013, which included integration of Paveway IV bombs and new secure communications from Cassidian in Phase A and Tactical Information Exchange (TIE) datalink from General Dynamics in Phase B. The GR1A reconnaissance variant, operated by the RAF and RSAF, used the TIRRS system and replaced the cannon; 30 GR1As were ordered, 14 as rebuilds and 16 new. When upgraded to GR4 standard, GR1As became GR4A, and with the shift from low-level to medium/high-level operations, the internal TIRRS was no longer used, leading the RAF's Tactical Reconnaissance Wing to operate both GR4A and GR4 aircraft. The Tornado ADV, operated by the RAF (designated F2 or F3), Saudi Arabia, and Italy, was developed as a long-endurance interceptor, not a dogfighter, with 80% parts commonality with the IDS, greater acceleration, improved RB199 Mk.104 engines, a stretched body, greater fuel capacity, AI.24 Foxhunter radar, and software changes, featuring only one cannon for an inflight refuelling probe. The ECR variant, operated by Germany and Italy, was designed for Suppression of Enemy Air Defences, equipped with radar detection and AGM-88 HARM anti-radiation missiles; the Luftwaffe received 35 new ECRs, Italy received 16 converted IDSs, Italian ECRs lacked built-in reconnaissance and used RecceLite pods, only Luftwaffe ECRs had the RB199 Mk.105 engine with higher thrust, and German ECRs did not carry a cannon. The RAF used the IDS version in the SEAD role and modified some Tornado F.3s for this mission. The GR4 was used in Operation Telic, Britain's contribution to the 2003 invasion of Iraq, with RAF Tornados flying alongside American aircraft in the opening phase, striking Iraqi targets, and deploying the Storm Shadow cruise missile for the first time to minimize civilian casualties. While 25% of UK air-launched weapons in Kosovo were precision-guided, this ratio increased to 85% in Iraq four years later. On 23 March 2003, a Tornado GR4 was shot down over Iraq by friendly fire from a US Patriot missile battery, killing both crew members; a US board of inquiry in July 2003 exonerated the operators, citing the Tornado's "lack of functioning IFF" as a factor, with problems in Patriot systems also suggested, including a fatal shootdown of a US Navy F/A-18 a few weeks later. Britain withdrew the last of its Tornados from Iraq in June 2009. In early 2009, several GR4s arrived at Kandahar Airfield, Afghanistan, to replace Harrier GR7/9 aircraft deployed since November 2004. In 2009, Paveway IV guided bombs were introduced on RAF Tornados, previously used by Harriers in Afghanistan. In summer 2010, extra Tornados were dispatched to Kandahar for the 2010 Afghan election. British Tornados ended operations in Afghanistan in November 2014, having flown over 5,000 pairs of sorties for 33,500 hours, including 600 "shows of force" to deter Taliban attacks, with over 70 engagements deploying 140 Brimstone missiles and Paveway IV bombs and over 3,000 27 mm cannon shells. Prior to the 2010 Strategic Defence and Security Review (SDSR), the Tornado's retirement was under consideration with £7.5 billion in anticipated savings; the SDSR retained the Tornado at the expense of the Harrier, with numbers declining as the fleet transitioned to Eurofighter Typhoon and F-35 Lightning II. By July 2013, 59 GR4s were receiving the CUSP avionics upgrade. On 18 March 2011, British Prime Minister David Cameron announced Tornados and Typhoons would enforce a no-fly zone in Libya; in March 2011, several Tornados flew 3,000-mile strike missions against targets inside Libya, the longest-range bombing mission by the RAF since the Falklands conflict, using laser-guided bombs and Brimstone missiles. In August 2014, Tornado GR4s were deployed to RAF Akrotiri, Cyprus, to support refugees from Islamic State militants in northern Iraq, following US air attacks; on 27 September 2014, after Parliament approved airstrikes in Iraq, two Tornados conducted their first armed reconnaissance mission with coalition aircraft, and the next day made the first airstrike on a heavy weapons post and armored vehicle, supporting Kurdish forces in northwest Iraq. By 1 March 2015, eight Tornados had been deployed to Akrotiri and conducted 159 airstrikes against IS targets in Iraq. On 2 December 2015, Parliament approved air strikes in Syria and Iraq to combat ISIL; Tornados began bombing that evening. On 14 April 2018, four Tornado GR4s from RAF Akrotiri struck a Syrian military facility with Storm Shadow cruise missiles in response to a suspected chemical attack on Douma by the Syrian regime. On 10 July 2018, nine Tornado GR4s from RAF Marham flew over London to celebrate 100 years of the RAF. In late 2018, the RAF commemorated the Tornado's service with three special schemes: ZG752 with green/grey camouflage, and ZG775 and ZD716 honoring the final operating units, No. IX (B) Squadron and No. 31 Squadron. On 31 January 2019, the Tornado GR4 flew its last operational sorties in Operation Shader. The eight Tornados from RAF Akrotiri returned to RAF Marham in early February 2019, their duties taken over by six Typhoons. Between September 2014 and January 2019, RAF Tornados accounted for 31% of the estimated 4,315 casualties inflicted on ISIL. On 19, 20, and 21 February 2019, flypasts were held over BAE Warton, RAF Honington, and RAF Lossiemouth to mark 40 years of service and retirement. On 28 February, nine Tornados flew a diamond nine formation flypast over a graduation parade at RAF Cranwell before returning and conducting passes over RAF Marham. On 14 March 2019, the final flight of an RAF Tornado was carried out by Tornado GR4 ZA463, the oldest remaining Tornado, over RAF Marham during the disbandment parade of No. IX (B) Squadron and No. 31 Squadron. The Tornado GR4 was officially retired from RAF service on 1 April 2019, the 101st anniversary of the RAF. Post-retirement, five Tornados returned to RAF Honington by road for the Complex Air Ground Environment (CAGE) training simulation. On 2 July 2023, pylons from decommissioned RAF Tornado GR4s were fitted to Ukrainian Su-24s to launch Storm Shadow missiles, with the Su-24s capable of carrying at least two Storm Shadows, requiring target coordinates to be entered before takeoff. In 1984, Royal Saudi Air Force pilots visited RAF Honington to evaluate the Tornado GR1. On 25 September 1985, the UK and Saudi Arabia signed the Al Yamamah I contract, including the sale of 48 IDS and 24 ADV Tornados. In October 1985, four RSAF crews joined the Tri-National Tornado Training Establishment at RAF Cottesmore. The first Saudi Tornado IDS (701) flew on 17 February 1986, and the first four IDS were delivered to King Abdul Aziz Air Base, Dharan on 26 March 1986. The first Saudi Tornado squadron, No. 7 Squadron, received 20 aircraft by 8 October 1987. The first Saudi ADV (2905) flew on 1 December 1988, with first deliveries arriving in Saudi Arabia on 20 March 1989. The first two RSAF ADV squadrons, Nos. 29 and 34, reached full strength of 12 aircraft each by 1990. In the run-up to the Gulf War, the RSAF pooled its Tornado squadrons, with a joint 24-aircraft ADV unit flying missions in Operation Desert Shield. Saudi Tornados participated in the Gulf War, with No. 7 Squadron conducting its first mission on the night of 17 January 1991; in total, the RSAF flew 665 IDS sorties and 451 ADV sorties, losing one IDS (765) on the night of 19/20 January. In June 1993, the Al Yamamah II contract was signed, including 48 additional IDSs. Following experience with the Tornado and F-15E, the RSAF discontinued low-level training in the F-15E due to the Tornado's superior low-altitude performance. Ten Saudi Tornados were fitted for reconnaissance missions. The 22 Tornado ADVs were replaced by the Eurofighter Typhoon; retired aircraft were purchased back by the UK. By 2007, both the Sea Eagle anti-ship missile and ALARM anti-radiation missile had been withdrawn from RSAF Tornado service. As of 2010, Saudi Arabia signed contracts for new weapon systems, including IRIS-T air-to-air, Brimstone, and Storm Shadow missiles. In September 2006, Saudi Arabia signed a £2.5 billion (US$4.7 billion) contract with BAE Systems to upgrade up to 80 RSAF Tornado IDS aircraft to remain in service until 2020 under the "Tornado Sustainment Programme" (TSP), to equip them with new precision-guided weapons and enhanced targeting equipment common with UK Tornado GR4 systems. The first RSAF Tornado was returned to BAE Systems Warton in December 2006 for upgrade, and the first modernized aircraft returned to Saudi Arabia in December 2007. Starting in November 2009, RSAF Tornados, along with F-15s, conducted air raids during the Shia insurgency in north Yemen, the first such operation since Operation Desert Storm in 1991. RSAF Tornados continue to play a central role in Saudi-led bombing campaigns in Yemen. On 7 January 2018, Houthi fighters claimed to have shot down a Saudi warplane conducting raids over northern Yemen; Saudi reports stated it was an RSAF Tornado lost for 'technical reasons' with both crew rescued. On 12 July 2018, another RSAF Tornado crashed in Asir region after returning from Saada, Yemen due to a technical malfunction. On 14 February 2020, a Saudi Tornado was shot down during a close air support mission in Yemen's Al Jouf governorate by Houthis; the next day, the Saudi command confirmed the loss, and a video showed the downing using a two-stage surface-to-air missile, with both pilots ejecting and being captured by Houthis.

The aircraft featured improvements such as increased acceleration, upgraded RB199 Mk.104 engines, a longer fuselage, enhanced fuel capacity, the AI.24 Foxhunter radar, and software updates. It was equipped with a single cannon to allow space for a retractable in-flight refuelling probe.
